challenges.title: SELECT and WHERE: Querying Your Data
description: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the universal language for working with relational databases. In 2026, SQL remains essential — PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and cloud databases like BigQuery, Snowflake, and Aurora all use it.
The most fundamental SQL operation is the SELECT statement:

-- Select all columns SELECT * FROM users; -- Select specific columns SELECT name, email FROM users; -- Filter with WHERE SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > 50000 AND department = 'Engineering'; -- Comparison operators: =, !=, >, <, >=, <=, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE SELECT * FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 50; SELECT * FROM users WHERE role IN ('admin', 'moderator'); SELECT * FROM posts WHERE title LIKE '%JavaScript%';
In JavaScript, the equivalent of SELECT is .map(), WHERE is .filter(), and SELECT column is accessing object properties.
Instructions

Write a function sqlSelect that takes an array of objects (rows), an array of column names (columns), and a predicate function (where). Return the filtered rows with only the specified columns. If columns is ['*'], return all columns.
challengeSeed: // Simulates: SELECT columns FROM table WHERE predicate
// 1. Filter rows using the where predicate
// 2. Map to only include specified columns (or all if columns=['*'])
tests: var data = [{id:1,name:'Alice',age:30,dept:'Eng'},{id:2,name:'Bob',age:25,dept:'HR'},{id:3,name:'Carol',age:35,dept:'Eng'}]; var r = sqlSelect(data, ['name','dept'], function(row) { return row.dept === 'Eng'; }); assert(r.length === 2 && r[0].name === 'Alice', 'message: Should filter to Eng department only.');
assert(r[0].age === undefined, 'message: Only selected columns should be present.');
var all = sqlSelect(data, ['*'], null); assert(all.length === 3 && all[0].age === 30, 'message: SELECT * should return all columns and rows.');

challenges.title: ORDER BY and LIMIT: Sorting and Paging Results
description: ORDER BY sorts query results by one or more columns. LIMIT restricts the number of returned rows — essential for pagination in web apps.

-- Sort by salary descending, then name ascending SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC, name ASC; -- Pagination: page 3, 10 items per page SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20; -- skip first 20, take next 10 -- Top 5 highest earners SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5;
LIMIT/OFFSET pagination is used in virtually every web application: news feeds, search results, product listings, user tables.
Instructions
Write a function sqlOrderLimit that takes rows, a sortKey string, a direction ('ASC' or 'DESC'), a limit number, and an offset number. Return the sorted, paged results.
challengeSeed: // Simulates: ORDER BY sortKey direction LIMIT limit OFFSET offset
function sqlOrderLimit(rows, sortKey, direction, limit, offset) {
// 1. Sort a copy of rows by sortKey
tests: var data = [{name:'Carol',salary:95000},{name:'Alice',salary:70000},{name:'Bob',salary:85000}]; var r = sqlOrderLimit(data, 'salary', 'DESC', 2, 0); assert(r[0].name === 'Carol' && r[1].name === 'Bob', 'message: DESC order should put highest salary first.');
var r2 = sqlOrderLimit(data, 'salary', 'ASC', 1, 1); assert(r2[0].name === 'Bob', 'message: ASC with offset=1 should skip Alice (lowest) and return Bob.');
assert(data[0].name === 'Carol', 'message: Original array should not be mutated.');

challenges.title: JOIN: Combining Data from Multiple Tables
description: JOIN is one of SQL's most powerful features — it combines rows from two tables based on a related column. Understanding joins is crucial for working with relational databases.

-- INNER JOIN: rows that match in both tables SELECT users.name, orders.total FROM users INNER JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id; -- LEFT JOIN: all users, even those without orders SELECT users.name, orders.total FROM users LEFT JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id; -- (orders.total will be NULL for users with no orders) -- SELF JOIN: a table joined with itself SELECT e.name as employee, m.name as manager FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
Join types: INNER JOIN (only matching rows), LEFT JOIN (all left rows + matching right), RIGHT JOIN (all right + matching left), FULL OUTER JOIN (all rows from both).
Instructions
Implement innerJoin that takes two arrays (tableA, tableB), and two key strings (keyA, keyB). Return an array of merged objects for rows where tableA[i][keyA] === tableB[j][keyB].
challengeSeed: // Simulates: SELECT * FROM tableA INNER JOIN tableB ON tableA.keyA = tableB.keyB
// If keys match, merge both rows and push to result
tests: var users = [{id:1,name:'Alice'},{id:2,name:'Bob'},{id:3,name:'Carol'}]; var orders = [{user_id:1,total:100},{user_id:1,total:200},{user_id:2,total:150}]; var joined = innerJoin(users, orders, 'id', 'user_id'); assert(joined.length === 3, 'message: Should return 3 joined rows (Alice has 2 orders, Bob has 1).');
assert(joined[0].name === 'Alice' && joined[0].total === 100, 'message: Merged row should have properties from both tables.');
assert(!joined.some(function(r) { return r.name === 'Carol'; }), 'message: Carol has no orders, should not appear in INNER JOIN.');

challenges.title: Aggregate Functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, GROUP BY
description: Aggregate functions compute a single result from multiple rows. Combined with GROUP BY, they produce per-group statistics — essential for analytics and reporting.

-- Count orders per user SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) as order_count FROM orders GROUP BY user_id; -- Average salary by department SELECT department, AVG(salary) as avg_salary, MAX(salary) as top_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department HAVING AVG(salary) > 80000; -- HAVING filters AFTER grouping -- Total revenue by month SELECT MONTH(created_at) as month, SUM(total) as revenue FROM orders GROUP BY MONTH(created_at) ORDER BY month;
HAVING is like WHERE but applied after GROUP BY — it filters groups, not rows.
Instructions

Write groupByAgg that takes rows, a groupKey to group by, and an aggFn function that receives an array of values and returns an aggregate. Also takes valueKey. Return an array of { group, aggregate } objects sorted by group name.
challengeSeed: // Simulates: SELECT groupKey, aggFn(valueKey) FROM rows GROUP BY groupKey
// Convert groups object to array of { group, aggregate } objects
tests: var data = [{dept:'Eng',salary:90000},{dept:'Eng',salary:100000},{dept:'HR',salary:65000},{dept:'HR',salary:70000}]; var sum = function(vals) { return vals.reduce(function(a,b){return a+b;},0); }; var r = groupByAgg(data, 'dept', 'salary', sum); assert(r.length === 2, 'message: Should have 2 groups.');
assert(r[0].group === 'Eng' && r[0].aggregate === 190000, 'message: Eng total salary should be 190000.');
assert(r[1].group === 'HR' && r[1].aggregate === 135000, 'message: HR total salary should be 135000.');
